source.title: scTab: Scaling cross-tissue single-cell annotation models
source.authors: Felix Fischer; David S. Fischer; R. Mukhin; A. Isaev; Evan Biederstedt; A. Villani; F. Theis

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies scaling in supervised single-cell classification, not language-model pretraining scaling laws. It cites language-model scaling work as context but does not test power-law fits, predict larger runs from smaller ones, or study compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports single-cell classifier results as training-data and parameter counts vary, including cross-entropy loss and macro F1. These are not language-model pretraining results and the paper does not test whether they follow the power-law forms in the claim. The scaling results are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version. Other benchmark comparisons are not included because they do not measure the claim's object.
record.test_reason: The study shows single-cell classifier (scTab) loss and macro F1 improving with training data (2.1–15.2M cells) and parameters (1.7–16.2M). It fits no power law, reports no exponent and makes no extrapolation, so its results cannot show whether the power-law form (V5) or any language-model version holds. Kaplan et al. is cited only as motivation. Its scaling findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that scTab's performance scales with training data size and model size, that data scaling is driven mainly by donor/batch diversity rather than cell count, and that nonlinear models outperform linear ones at scale.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses supervised single-cell classification and does not implement or fit the language-model pretraining scaling-law recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Data-scaling outcome differs between donor-based subsampling and random cell-based subsampling.

fits_no_version.finding: Donor-based data subsampling gives strong scaling of test loss and macro F1. Random cell-based subsampling gives much weaker scaling (Fig. 2b).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In single-cell classification, data scaling gains depend on donor/batch diversity rather than raw cell count.

fits_no_version.finding: scTab macro F1 rises from 0.7864 to 0.8323 as parameters grow from 1.7M to 16.2M on the full dataset (Fig. 2f).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger scTab models achieve higher macro F1 in cross-tissue cell type classification.

fits_no_version.finding: Data scaling holds across all organ systems. The F1 gain from 2.1M to 15.2M cells has a minimum of 0.0454 and a median of 0.1219 (Fig. 2c).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data-scaling gains vary in size across organ systems.

fits_no_version.finding: The linear baseline's learning curve flattens earlier than scTab's (Fig. 2d). scTab exceeds it by 0.0447 F1 at full data. No row records this.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Nonlinear models keep benefiting from more data where linear models plateau in single-cell classification.

record.problems: No power-law fits, fitted exponents, or extrapolation tests are reported. The scaling experiments use cross-tissue single-cell classification metrics rather than language-model pretraining loss. Several scaling-curve values are presented only in figures.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss; no power-law fit in parameters, data or compute.
No extrapolation from small runs to larger ones.
No depth/width shape comparison at fixed parameter count; only hidden-unit size is varied.
The study works in a new modality (single-cell RNA-seq classification) but does not fit or test a power-law form. Curves are figure-only with five data points and a sevenfold data range.
No downstream-task prediction from scale or pretraining loss.
No fitted exponents or fitting-choice comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The study uses 'scaling' informally: monotonic improvement over a narrow range, with no power-law form. The record's relation and tranche are kept. Rows r5 and r6 should be merged or cross-referenced as one contrast.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation from small language-model runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and architecture details at fixed parameter count for language models.
The paper studies single-cell classification scaling but does not test whether the same power-law form holds in that setting or another modality/training regime.
Predictability of downstream task performance with language-model scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices, including whether curves bend away from power laws.

relation.reason: The paper cites language-model scaling laws as motivation and discusses future scaling-law research, without testing or using a fitted scaling law.

tranche.reason: The study measures supervised classification improvements with dataset and model size, without establishing a power-law form, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or downstream scaling from pretraining. These results fit none of the listed claim versions.

source_check.notes: Observed and partial describe generic performance scaling and its weaker cell-subsampling control, not evidence for a claim version. All Fig. 2 models were trained without data augmentation; the authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased.
